articles.title: Cradle-to-gate life cycle assessment of pasteurized milk production in Uzbekistan identifies environmental hotspots and improvement opportunities
articles.desc: Dairy production is an important component of Uzbekistan's food system but is associated with environmental burdens. This study presents a cradle-to-gate life cycle assessment (LCA) of pasteurized milk production in Uzbekistan to quantify environmental impacts, identify hotspots, evaluate uncertaint
articles.content: Dairy production is an important component of Uzbekistan's food system but is associated with environmental burdens. This study presents a cradle-to-gate life cycle assessment (LCA) of pasteurized milk production in Uzbekistan to quantify environmental impacts, identify hotspots, evaluate uncertainty, and assess environmental improvement options. A case-based inventory informed by farm records and national production data was developed for 1000 kg of pasteurized milk at the factory gate, covering feed production, dairy farming, transport, processing, and packaging. Environmental impacts were assessed using ReCiPe 2016 Midpoint (H). Global warming potential (GWP), characterized water consumption, terrestrial acidification, freshwater eutrophication, and fossil resource scarcity were 1537.8 kg CO2-eq, 1509.5 m3, 13.40 kg SO2-eq, 0.775 kg P-eq, and 158.1 kg oil-eq, respectively. Dairy-farm activities were the largest GWP contributor (46.6%), while feed production accounted for all characterized water consumption and dominated freshwater eutrophication (81.8%). Feed production and dairy-farm activities contributed 52.9% and 47.1% of terrestrial acidification, respectively, whereas packaging dominated fossil resource scarcity (65.8%). Monte Carlo analysis quantified model uncertainty, while sensitivity analysis identified methane/manure emissions as the main GWP uncertainty driver, irrigation demand for water consumption, fertilizer nutrient losses for acidification and eutrophication, and packaging factors for fossil resource scarcity. The integrated inventory-level sustainability scenario reduced GWP, water consumption, acidification, eutrophication, and fossil resource scarcity by 23.9%, 47.5%, 25.0%, 25.0%, and 4.5%, respectively. These findings support impact-specific strategies for improving the environmental sustainability of the assessed dairy production system and provide evidence relevant to dairy-sector improvement in Uzbekistan.

articles.content: Food aid enrollment tanks after SNAP rule changes – Longmont Times-Call By Halle Parker, Verite News, KFF Health News After President Donald Trump signed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act more than a year ago, enrollment in the federal food assistance program dropped rapidly across the nation as states enforced new restrictions and prepared to take on more of the costs. were enrolled in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, also known as SNAP or food stamps, this June than in July 2025, when the law was enacted. Louisiana saw one of the most precipitous declines, dropping about 170,000 people, or 21% of state enrollees, according to federal data. “We haven’t seen a decline of this magnitude in about three decades,” said , senior director of research on food assistance at the left-leaning Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, which did the analysis. from August 2025 to this August, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture. Elected officials, policy analysts, and anti-hunger advocates are pressing Congress to delay provisions in the law that will cut federal funding for food benefits and steeply increase the cost for states. They want to insert the delay in the Farm Bill, which is pending in the Senate. The provisions required states to start paying for 75% of the cost to operate SNAP on Oct. 1. Previously, the USDA and states split SNAP’s administration cost 50-50. Beginning in October 2027, some states may also have to cover part of the cost of SNAP benefits that had been paid fully by the federal government. The amount that a state pays toward benefits will depend on its , or how often it underpays or overpays enrollees. The higher the error rate, the higher the state’s share of SNAP benefit costs. In Louisiana, the state may have to cover up to $199 million of the cost for benefits, according to an analysis by the . Its error rate increased from 6.62% in fiscal year 2024 to 8.14% in FY 2025, the most recent data available. Many states, including Louisiana, have placed pressure on applicants to submit more information more often to verify their eligibility to reduce the state’s payment error rate and limit how much the cost of benefits shifts to the state. “It’s been a race to drive down those error rates,” Llobrera said. He said the challenge of implementing new program restrictions and requiring more documentation has increased the burden on applicants and state agencies. The agencies have to process more paperwork on a tight timeline without enough staff. This can increase the likelihood of errors when processing applications, potentially leading to rejection of benefits for more people. It’s also harder for applicants to meet additional verification requirements. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act expanded work requirements for SNAP, made it harder for states to waive the work requirements, and revoked access for many noncitizens with legal status. The Louisiana Department of Health did not respond to requests for comment. Tia Fields, the safety net policy analyst for the nonpartisan Invest in Louisiana think tank, said the cost increase to the state has contributed to two crises: a projected shortfall in the state budget and eligible families’ losing access to help. In Louisiana, state data shows that 75% of people who lost SNAP from July 2025 to June 2026 did so for . When the program’s strict deadlines for documentation and verification aren’t met, applications and renewals are closed. Fields said applicants may miss forms and interviews or fail to recertify or report changes in their status. Other times, the problem is on the state’s side. Agency notices may reach applicants past the deadline due to mail delays, they may be sent to the wrong address, or caseworkers may have backlogs in processing paperwork. “Families are still hungry, and they’re actually eligible for the program,” Fields said. “This is a tax bill that we really cannot afford.” The additional administrative burden and the financial penaltie

articles.title: Bolt Graphics seeks $100M at $700M valuation to challenge Nvidia and AMD with its Zeus GPU
articles.desc: Bolt Graphics has spent roughly six years designing a graphics chip, and the only silicon it has to…
articles.content: Bolt Graphics seeks $100M at $700M valuation to challenge Nvidia and AMD with its Zeus GPU — TFN Bolt Graphics seeks $100M at $700M valuation to challenge Nvidia and AMD with its Zeus GPU Reuters reports Bolt Graphics is seeking about $100M at a valuation of roughly $700M. Its Zeus GPU exists only as a small test chip, with production targeted for late 2027. Reuters could not identify a lead investor, and the amount and price could still change. has spent roughly six years designing a graphics chip, and the only silicon it has to show for it is a test chip measuring six square millimetres. that the Sunnyvale, California, startup is trying to raise about $100M at a valuation of about $700M, citing three people familiar with the matter. The round tests whether investors will fund chips that are not built for artificial intelligence. Nvidia and AMD have poured billions of dollars into AI-focused products. Bolt is designing its Zeus graphics processing unit (GPU) for scientific computing, chip design, and professional rendering, work that includes calculations known as FP64, a more exact kind of maths than gaming usually needs. It plans to start with 3D artists and game developers before moving into gaming GPUs. founded Bolt in 2020. When it introduced Zeus in early 2025, it claimed up to 10 times the path-tracing speed of Nvidia’s RTX 5090, a rendering method that simulates how light behaves. The claim drew because the company had no working silicon. It still had none at CES in January, when it showed a prototype card. In April, Bolt finished the design of a test chip on a 12-nanometre process from Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC). On October 13, it said it had completed the first round of testing and opened an office in Taipei to work with its manufacturing partners, The test chip hardwires one task: solving Maxwell’s equations, which describe electromagnetic fields and underpin electromagnetic simulation. The commercial chip is a different object. Bolt plans a design of about 400 square millimetres on TSMC’s five-nanometre process, built from several smaller chips with a processor integrated. Bolt says production starts in the fourth quarter of 2027. HPCwire says the finished GPU is not expected to ship until 2028. Bolt also says Zeus can cut the cost of computing by up to 17 times, that its sales pipeline exceeds $500M, and that more than 14,000 people have joined its early-access programme. None of those figures has been independently verified. A $700M price tag for a chip due in 2027 or 2028 closed more than $97M at a $650M valuation on September 29, led by TQ Ventures. The company says its Electron E1 chip is in volume production, though it has not disclosed revenue. Bolt is asking for almost the same money at a slightly higher price with a test chip. That is not a verdict, because valuations at this stage are set on teams and plans. is reportedly raising at about $2.5B with no product, and doubled to $21B in August after Jane Street, which led the round, became its first production customer. What Bolt has not made public is how much it has raised so far. Crunchbase lists a Series A, and Tom’s Hardware reported that round was oversubscribed, but the amount and lead investor were never disclosed. That leaves no way to measure the step-up a $700M price implies. articles.title: Sunlight gives biodiesel by-product a second life as hydrogen and valuable chemicals
articles.desc: Key Points Sunlight can covert glycerol, a low value product of biodiesel production into hydrogen and higher value chemicals A photocatalyst based on
articles.content: Sunlight gives biodiesel by-product a second life as hydrogen and valuable chemicals | The National Tribune Sunlight can covert glycerol, a low value product of biodiesel production into hydrogen and higher value chemicals A photocatalyst based on zinc indium sulfide, modified with very small amounts of nickel and cobalt, increased the hydrogen evolution rate and the production of glyceraldehyde and dihydroxyacetone The research team used X-ray absorption spectroscopy and infrared microspectroscopy at the Australian Synchrotron to observe the catalytic reactions in real time Australian researchers and international collaborators have demonstrated a solar-driven approach to convert glycerol, a low-value by-product of biodiesel production, into hydrogen and higher-value chemicals. Using advanced techniques at Australian Synchrotron, they revealed how the catalyst changes while it was working. The study, led by researchers at the University of New South Wales, investigated a process known as photoreforming, in which light energy is used to drive chemical reactions to simultaneously produce hydrogen and transform organic feedstocks into useful products. The was published in Applied Catalysis B: Environment and Energy. Glycerol is produced in large quantities by the growing biodiesel industry, with approximately 100 kilograms generated for every tonne of biodiesel. Crude glycerol can be worth as little as US$0.11 per kilogram. Chemicals can be produced from it, such as glyceraldehyde and dihydroxyacetone, which have applications in the chemical and pharmaceutical industries, valued at approximately US$75 and US$150 per kilogram, respectively. Dr Denny Gunawan from UNSW said the opportunity was to use sunlight not only to produce hydrogen, but also to extract greater value from an existing industrial by-product. “Rather than using an expensive feedstock simply to produce hydrogen, photoreforming gives us the opportunity to do two useful things at once; generate hydrogen and convert a low-value by-product into more valuable chemicals,” said Dr Gunawan. “The challenge is that glycerol can follow several different reaction pathways. If we understand what controls those pathways, we can start designing catalysts that steer the reaction towards the products we want.” The researchers developed a photocatalyst based on zinc indium sulfide, which was modified with very small amounts of nickel and cobalt. Under visible light, adding the nickel-cobalt cocatalyst increased the hydrogen evolution rate by approximately ten times compared with the unmodified material. It also changed the chemistry of the reaction, substantially increasing the proportion of glycerol converted through pathways producing glyceraldehyde and dihydroxyacetone. Tests under simulated sunlight demonstrated the simultaneous production of hydrogen and useful organic products with the catalyst achieving a hydrogen production rate competitive with other reported solar-driven glycerol photoreforming systems. To understand why nickel and cobalt changed the reaction, researchers needed to observe the catalyst while it was actually operating. At the X-ray Absorption Spectroscopy (XAS) Beamline, the researchers used two techniques, in situ XAS and Fixed Energy XAS (FE-XAS), to investigate what happened to the nickel and cobalt sites when the photocatalyst was illuminated. By measuring at selected X-ray energies rather than scanning across the full absorption spectrum, FE-XAS can follow changes in the catalyst much faster than conventional XAS. ANSTO Principal Scientist Bernt Johannessen said the ability to follow the catalyst dynamically provided information that could not be obtained simply by examining it before and after the reaction. “Using these advanced capabilities, we could follow the nickel and cobalt sites as the catalyst responded to illumination and observe changes that occurred in less than one second,” said Dr Johannessen. “When the light was switched on, we could se

articles.title: Want your AI chats to stay private? Brave TEEs up end-to-end encryption
articles.desc: Browser maker using trusted hardware to protect conversations with GLM 5.3 Flash
articles.content: Want your AI chats to stay private? Brave TEEs up end-to-end encryption Want your AI chats to stay private? Brave TEEs up end-to-end encryption Browser maker using trusted hardware to protect conversations with GLM 5.3 Flash Benchmarked: Nvidia's RTX Spark notebook delivers serious local AI compute, at a price $24,000 AI experiment ports TypeScript compiler to Rust TSMC sends scouts to check whether America's datacenters can deliver Linux kernel devs drop obligatory confession of AI tool usage Researchers cig-nal their faith in AI by taking up smoking Brave Software has set up a secure space so those using its browser can converse with the company's AI assistant in private. At a time when AI agents like Meta's Muse ask for to personal information, and AI companies , this amounts to swimming against the tide. to implement a confidential channel for LLM conversations with the help of NEAR AI's trusted execution environment (TEE), the browser maker has connected its Leo AI assistant to 's GLM 5.3 Flash under the protection of end-to-end encryption. The result is that Brave users can submit a prompt to Leo that gets encrypted on-device and sent over the network using , a protocol for separating network requests from associated content. forwards the encrypted query to the TEE without passing along the user's IP address. After Brave verifies the enclave's attestation, the browser encrypts the query using a key bound to the TEE. The TEE decrypts the request, runs it through the AI model, and sends back an encrypted response that gets decrypted by the receiving browser. ' that users shouldn't have to place blind trust in the software they rely on," said Brendan Eich, co-founder and CEO of Brave, in . "They should be able to verify it; this is a user-first principle. AI has raised the stakes, yet too much of it still runs on 'trust me bro' promises, often at the user's expense." NEAR AI's confidential AI pipeline is built with Intel TDX and Nvidia Confidential Compute. It includes end-to-end encryption that keeps Brave from knowing what was asked and NEAR AI from knowing who did the asking during the network hop. Data isolation prevents the prompt or response from being read during processing. Responses are signed in the TEE and there's attestation so users can confirm there's no Leo's GLM 5.3 Flash brain may be isolated in this scenario, but Brave's AI bot can still conduct searches from within the TEE via the Brave Search API's LLM context endpoint. And any searches done this way transit via the TEE rather than the user's browser, which keeps the user's IP address out of the picture. The implementation isn't quite complete: Brave intends to work on moving the verification step into the browser and to publish a log of TEE keys, and to provide enclave attestation for exact model weights loaded into memory, among other things. Brave is not the only company trying to make AI less of a data exposure risk. all have some form of private cloud compute infrastructure for AI. , which promises encrypted inference, not to mention providers advertising zero data retention, which isn't as verifiable. One way to ensure privacy while using AI is to run inference on local hardware using an open weight model, assuming the model and the machine running it haven't been compromised. ® Open-weight models win hearts, minds, and wallets They handle 71.5% of Vercel gateway tokens and nearly a quarter of estimated spending Benchmarked: Nvidia's RTX Spark notebook delivers serious local AI compute, at a price El Reg digs its claws into HP's N1X-powered OmniBook Ultra 16 PARTNER CONTENT: A million reasons why advanced computing matters for genomics Node.js creator ditches Deno to work on open source Cloudflare Workers You're building servers 'wrong,' says Ryan Dahl as Cloudflare gobbles his Deno startup It won't kill you, or humanity, to get off the AI upgrade treadmill New models arrive so fast, we already have more new tech than it's possible to understand in

The result of this research does not constitute investment advice or an invitation to conclude certain stock exchange transactions. Classification of Sphene Capital GmbH to Eloro Resources Ltd Encouraging results from the expansion diamond drilling program Eloro's recent announcement represents a meaningful step towards geological rather than economic de-risking. The results are particularly encouraging because they combine attractive grades of silver and tin with significant drilled widths and relatively shallow mineralisation and the possibility of incorporating higher-grade material into an initial open-pit mining operation. Iska Iska's principal challenge, in our view, is therefore no longer demonstrating the existence of a large mineralised system but establishing that a commercially attractive portion of this system can be mined, processed, and financed under realistic technical and economic assumptions. We maintain our Buy rating and our price target of CAD 18.00 per share. Our price target is purely based on the in-situ valuation of the Santa Barbara Breccia Pipe within the Iska Iska property in Bolivia, while excluding all other assets. Eloro's latest exploration results from its Iska Iska silver-tin polymetallic project provide additional evidence that the Santa Barbara mineralised system contains substantial near-surface, higher-grade mineralisation within a much larger, lower-grade polymetallic deposit. The most important finding (drillhole DSB-96, the most significant of the three reported holes) is the intersection of 87.10 metres grading 73.26 grams per tonne (g/t) silver and 0.18% tin, accompanied by a separate, particularly attractive interval of 17.90 metres grading 190.50 g/t silver and 0.45% tin. The reported silver grades are significantly above the 40 g/t silver grade reported for the Indicated Mineral Resource in April 2026, suggesting that the economic viability of Iska Iska may depend disproportionately on identifying, delineating, and selectively developing higher-grade zones rather than attempting to exploit the entire mineralised system. The recent findings are therefore not only strategically relevant because they may help increase the proportion of higher-grade material within the more confidently defined resource inventory; they are also encouraging because they demonstrate that higher silver grades are not confined to narrow, isolated structures. Instead, significant mineralisation occurs across considerable drilled intervals, potentially supporting the interpretation of a broad, structurally controlled hydrothermal system with multiple mineralising events. In addition, the reported intervals suggest that the near-surface mineralisation may contain a particularly high-grade component within a broader mineralised envelope. If this interpretation is confirmed, the possibility of selectively extracting higher-value material during the initial years of production could become a meaningful economic advantage for Eloro Resources, in our view.
